strengths: The UIQ benchmark is a well-motivated contribution: query-type robustness (questions, imperatives, keyphrases, paraphrases, exclusionary/negative queries) is a genuinely underexplored evaluation dimension for audio-text retrieval, and the taxonomy is grounded in prior findings on real-world query patterns (Weck & Font 2024; Penha et al. 2022).

The data-leakage analysis (Appendix B) is thorough and independently valuable: quantifying that 17.7% of AudioCaps test clips and 61.0% of Clotho evaluation clips appear in WavCaps is an important service to the audio retrieval community, and the paper responds responsibly by applying blocklists and adding the leakage-free MECAT evaluation.

Evaluation claims are unusually honest for a systems paper: the authors openly state that M2D-CLAP is better on in-domain T2A and best Avg UIQ, positioning OEA's advantages only in T2T retrieval and hard negative discrimination rather than overclaiming overall superiority.

Breadth of experiments is adequate: six OEA variants across three backbones from two organizations, four CLAP baselines, vanilla LALM controls, efficiency benchmarking, and per-dataset/per-query-type breakdowns in the appendix.

The hard negative mining pipeline (acoustic similarity + semantic dissimilarity + human verification) is a sensible design that reduces single-embedding-model bias, and the proposed HNSR/TFR/∆-Rank metrics address a real limitation of standard R@k for exclusionary queries.

Reproducibility is supported by released checkpoints, prompts, generation parameters, evaluation protocols, and a web demo, with candid acknowledgment in the Limitations section (single generator LLM, memory requirements, MGA-CLAP/BGE filtering bias).
weaknesses: No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals anywhere. The headline claims rest on small margins (+4.3%p HNSR@10, +5.1%p Imperative) computed on small evaluation sets (847–1,045 clips), and several per-dataset tables (e.g., Tables 12–15) show OEA and M2D-CLAP trading wins with differences likely within noise; the paper's conclusions would be considerably more convincing with significance analysis.

Metric definitions are inconsistent between the main text and appendix: Section 3.3 defines HNSR@k as 'target retrieved in top-k AND hard negative outside top-k', while Appendix L defines HNSR as 'Rank(HN) > Rank(T)'. These are different quantities, yet both are reported and claimed to 'confirm the pattern', which undermines confidence in the discrimination analysis.

Fairness of the baseline comparison is not fully controlled: OEA is trained on WavCaps + AudioCaps (+Clotho) with LoRA on LLM backbones, while the CLAP baselines use different training corpora and budgets. The paper attributes OEA's T2T/discrimination advantages to the LLM backbone, but a stronger control (e.g., the same contrastive training recipe on a non-LLM encoder of comparable capacity, or an LLM with a separate audio front-end) is missing, so the causal claim 'LLM backbones provide superior semantic understanding' remains a hypothesis.

The hypothesized mechanism for OEA's exclusionary-query advantage (LLM pretraining exposure to negation patterns) is speculative and untested: there is no ablation (e.g., adding negative queries to training, probing negation handling directly) supporting it, and the paper itself notes OEA was never trained on UIQs, so the compositional-structure explanation is unverified.

There are apparent data inconsistencies in the tables: Robust-CLAP and LAION-CLAP produce essentially identical T2T numbers (Table 3: identical rows 50.05/65.88/72.67; Table 11 nearly identical), and several exact-duplicate values appear across OEA variants and datasets in Tables 13 and 15 (e.g., repeated 24.41/34.55, 8.25/36.20), suggesting copy errors or an evaluation pipeline issue that needs checking.

UIQ construction has acknowledged but non-trivial validity risks: queries are generated by a single LLM (GPT-5.1), constrained to ±2 words of original caption length—which conflicts with the paper's own cited evidence that real queries average 1.8 tokens—and negative queries are grounded in hard negatives mined with MGA-CLAP (the model that scores worst on HNSR), creating potential circularity between benchmark construction and model ranking. Human validation covers only 75 samples (15 per query type), a thin basis for the reported Likert means.

Section F ('Detailed Baseline Results') and G ('Detailed UIQ Results') contain subsection headings but appear to lack their described content in the manuscript, which is a completeness/clarity issue for the camera-ready version.
Full UIQ datasets are only promised 'upon publication', with sample subsets released now, which limits immediate reproducibility of the central benchmark.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the gap between caption-style benchmark queries and real-world search behavior is supported by prior work (Weck & Font 2024; NevIR; ExcluIR), and the UIQ taxonomy (conversational, reformulation, exclusionary) is linguistically sensible.

The data leakage analysis (Appendix B) is a genuine service to the community: documenting 17.7% AudioCaps and 61.0% Clotho overlap with WavCaps, with concrete ID-level examples, and evaluating on MECAT as a contamination-free benchmark.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental design: three backbone scales from two organizations, six OEA variants, four CLAP baselines, vanilla LALM baselines isolating the effect of retrieval training, and an efficiency/deployment analysis.

The hard negative mining pipeline combines acoustic and semantic filtering with human verification, reducing single-embedding-model bias, and the proposed HNSR/TFR metrics are clearly defined and address a real limitation of R@k.
Good release plan: checkpoints, web demo, UIQ benchmark datasets, generation prompts, and validation protocols are documented, supporting reproducibility.
The paper is candid about limitations (backbone dependence, memory cost, synthetic query generation, hard-negative coverage).
weaknesses: The headline claims are weaker than advertised. On the core T2A task OEA is only 'comparable' to M2D-CLAP (M2D-CLAP wins AudioCaps). The +22% relative T2T gain is on one dataset (MECAT R@5), is largely expected from swapping a small CLAP text encoder for a multi-billion-parameter LLM, and the abstract's 'dominant' framing overstates the effect (Figure 1 reports only +5.5 absolute mean R@5).

The +4.3%p HNSR@10 improvement is modest, and no statistical significance testing or variance across runs is reported anywhere in the paper; several margins between OEA variants and baselines are small relative to plausible seed variance.

Capacity confound is not controlled: OEA backbones are 3B-7B LLMs vs ~89-158M CLAP models. The paper attributes T2T/hard-negative gains to 'semantic understanding of LLM backbones' but offers no capacity-matched baseline or controlled experiment to isolate semantic capability from raw parameter count.

Apparent data errors undermine confidence in the results: Table 13's MECAT column contains repeated identical values across different models (e.g., 24.41, 34.55, 35.61 appearing multiple times), and similar duplication appears in Table 12; Table 3's LAION-CLAP and Robust-CLAP T2T rows are nearly identical. Appendices F and G are placeholder stubs with no content.

The UIQ benchmark is synthetic (GPT-5.1 generated) with thin human validation (75 samples, 675 ratings, 9 annotators); negative queries—the paper's key differentiator—receive the lowest validity score (3.82). The Appendix I argument against LLM-generation bias is partly circular (reasoning from the observed result pattern rather than independent evidence).

The claim that hard-negative discrimination 'emerges without explicit UIQ training' is confounded: OEA's training data, curriculum, and contrastive setup differ from M2D-CLAP's, so the source of the discrimination advantage is not isolated.

While blocklists are said to be applied for the WavCaps overlap, the amount of training data removed and the resulting impact are not quantified, leaving uncertainty about how contaminated the reported Clotho/AudioCaps OEA results remain.
Bibliography quality issues (e.g., 'Anonymous Wu and 1 others. 2025', 'Wenhao Zhang and 1 others') and repeated R@5/R@10 values across model rows suggest insufficient care in the final manuscript.

Novelty is incremental: adapting instruction-tuned multimodal LLMs with LoRA + InfoNCE for contrastive retrieval is a straightforward recipe; the primary contributions are the benchmark and metrics, whose validation is comparatively light.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important evaluation gap: caption-style benchmarks may overestimate audio-text retrieval capability, and the UIQ taxonomy (conversational, reformulation, exclusionary) is a reasonable and linguistically motivated decomposition of real-world query behavior.

The data leakage analysis (Appendix B) is a notable contribution in itself: quantifying that 17.7% of AudioCaps test clips and 61.0% of Clotho evaluation clips overlap with WavCaps is valuable for the community, and the authors both apply blocklists to their own training and add a leakage-free benchmark (MECAT).

The proposed discrimination metrics (HNSR@k, TFR, Delta-Rank) address a real shortcoming of standard R@k metrics, and the hard negative mining pipeline combines acoustic and semantic filtering with human verification, reducing single-embedding-model bias.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: three backbone scales from two organizations (Nemotron-3B, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B/7B), baseline CLAP variants including the current SOTA (M2D-CLAP), vanilla LALM ablations isolating the effect of retrieval training, an efficiency/deployment analysis, and a UIQ generation-distribution sanity check (Appendix I).

Reproducibility is strong: checkpoints, web demo, UIQ benchmark samples, generation prompts, parameters, and Likert scale definitions are all documented, and the claims in the abstract/conclusion are carefully hedged (e.g., 'comparable' T2A rather than overclaiming).
The writing is honest about trade-offs: M2D-CLAP wins in-domain T2A and Avg UIQ, OEA wins T2T and hard negative discrimination, and the Limitations section is substantive.
weaknesses: Several results tables show near-identical or exactly duplicated rows for LAION-CLAP and Robust-CLAP (e.g., Table 3 Clotho and MECAT columns are identical: 50.05/65.88/72.67 and 18.06/39.35/50.57; Table 11 is nearly the same). This strongly suggests an evaluation or transcription error for at least one baseline, and undermines confidence in the baseline numbers as reported.

Appendices F and G are empty placeholders ('This section provides...') despite being cross-referenced from the main text, and the release URL is truncated/blank in multiple places (footnote 1, conclusion). The manuscript is not fully polished.

No statistical significance testing is reported. Key headline gains are modest or inconsistent (Avg UIQ: OEA-Qwen3B(+Cl) 47.18 vs. M2D-CLAP 47.76, i.e., a loss; T2A gains concentrated in single variants), and with six OEA variants across three datasets, best-per-column cherry-picking is a concern. Variance over seeds is not reported.

A plausible confound for the UIQ results is not fully resolved: queries are generated by GPT-5.1, and LLM-based encoders may match GPT-generated phrasing better than CLAP's text encoders. Appendix I's argument (M2D-CLAP still wins Question/Keyphrase/Paraphrase) is suggestive but informal, and the ±2-word length constraint means the benchmark does not reflect the 1.8-token real Freesound queries the paper cites as motivation.

Human validation of the UIQ benchmark is small: 75 samples, 9 annotators, 675 ratings, with only 'moderate Human-LLM agreement' vaguely characterized (only one correlation coefficient reported; the promised KL-divergence comparison is never given). Negative queries score lowest (3.82/5), yet they anchor the paper's central discrimination claims.

Fairness of baseline comparison is partially confounded by training data: baselines likely trained on contaminated WavCaps data (inflating AudioCaps/Clotho numbers per the paper's own analysis), while OEA was trained on blocklisted data; conversely OEA uses far larger backbones (~3-7B vs. 89-158M). The paper discusses neither confound quantitatively when interpreting the T2T and discrimination gains.

The architectural novelty is limited: the method is LoRA-based contrastive adaptation of existing multimodal LLMs with a projection head and InfoNCE loss; the contribution rests mainly on the benchmark, metrics, and analysis rather than a new technique.

The central finding on hard negative discrimination could be sensitive to how negatives were mined (seeded by MGA-CLAP embeddings); although human verification mitigates this, no sensitivity analysis of the mining pipeline is provided.

strengths: Careful and unusually honest evaluation methodology: the paper self-identifies significant data leakage between WavCaps training data and standard benchmarks (17.7% of AudioCaps test, 61.0% of Clotho eval), applies blocklists, and adds the contamination-free MECAT benchmark—this is a genuinely useful contribution to audio retrieval evaluation practice.

The UIQ benchmark is a thoughtful response to a documented gap (caption-style queries vs. real search behavior), with a linguistically motivated taxonomy of five query types, released datasets, and both human (9 annotators, 675 ratings) and LLM validation.

Novel discrimination metrics (HNSR, TFR, ∆-Rank) address a real limitation of R@k: standard metrics cannot measure suppression of acoustically confusable distractors, which is the core challenge of exclusionary queries.

The mechanism ablations (Appendix O) are exemplary: audio-only separation tests, negation on/off controls, word-order shuffles with cross-model controls, and paired statistical tests. Critically, the authors let the evidence overturn their initial hypothesis (negation understanding from instruction tuning) in favor of a more defensible claim (audio-side separation). This raises confidence in the paper's central claims.
Multi-backbone validation (Nemotron-3B, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B/7B) across two organizations, plus an honest inference-efficiency analysis, strengthens generality claims and practical relevance.

Claims are calibrated relative to evidence: the paper does not overstate T2A gains (M2D-CLAP remains best on AudioCaps) and correctly attributes the sharper wins to T2T retrieval and hard-negative discrimination.
Good reproducibility posture: code, checkpoints, UIQ datasets, prompts, generation parameters, and detailed appendices are released.
weaknesses: The UIQ benchmark is synthetic (GPT-5.1 generated) and only 75 of 13,053 queries were human-validated. The authors acknowledge this, but the benchmark's claim to represent 'user intent' is weakened by the fact that real search queries average ~1.8 tokens (Weck and Font, 2024), far shorter than the 8–25 word UIQ formulations; only the keyphrase type approximates real query distributions.

Hard negative pairs are mined using MGA-CLAP, so 'hardness' is defined by that model's embedding space; OEA is evaluated on pairs constructed by one of its own baselines. The dual-model filtering and human threshold calibration mitigate but do not eliminate this circularity concern.

The T2T advantage (+22% relative on MECAT, +8.67 R@1 on Clotho) is somewhat expected given OEA's billion-parameter LLM text encoder vs. CLAP's small text towers, and the Clotho T2T gains are on a dataset the authors themselves show is 61% contaminated—the fairness of baseline training (same blocklists?) is not fully clarified.

Headline T2A results are only 'comparable' to M2D-CLAP, so the model contribution rests on narrower differentiators (T2T, HNSR@10 +4.3%p); the abstract's framing slightly outpaces the strength of these deltas, and significance testing is limited to ablations, not the main retrieval comparisons.

The unified-encoder novelty is modest: the work largely consists of LoRA-adapting existing native-audio multimodal LLMs (including Omni-Embed-Nemotron, itself a retrieval model) with a standard InfoNCE objective; the benchmark and metrics, not the architecture, carry the contribution.
Human-LLM validation agreement is described as 'moderate' overall and annotation volume is small, leaving benchmark validity partially assumed rather than established.

Exclusionary query performance remains low in absolute terms for all models (HNSR@10 ~21–35%), and the finding that the exclusion clause lexically pulls models toward the excluded clip is interesting but suggests the benchmark may partly measure a lexical artifact.

strengths: Thorough and genuinely useful data-leakage analysis (Appendix B): quantified overlap between WavCaps and AudioCaps (17.7%) and Clotho (61.0%) evaluation sets, with a principled mitigation (blocklists) and adoption of MECAT as a leakage-free benchmark—this is a contribution of independent value to the community

Extensive supporting material: three backbones from two organizations, ablations (Appendix O) that go beyond surface-level claims and honestly revise the paper's own mechanism hypothesis (the negation advantage is attributed to audio-side separation plus shared order sensitivity, not a unique LLM capability), inference-efficiency analysis, and human calibration of hard negative mining

Well-motivated evaluation gap: the mismatch between caption-style benchmark queries and real-world search behavior is documented with prior evidence, and the UIQ taxonomy (conversational, reformulation, exclusionary) is a reasonable organizing framework

The introduction of discrimination-focused metrics (HNSR@k, Δ-Rank, TFR) is a valid point—standard R@k does not capture whether models suppress confusable distractors, and Figure 3 explains this clearly

Strong reproducibility posture: released benchmark datasets, code, checkpoints, web demo, prompts, and hyperparameters; statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank, paired tests) reported for key ablations
weaknesses: Headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. On the core task (text-to-audio retrieval), M2D-CLAP still wins on AudioCaps and OEA's advantages concentrate on T2T retrieval—a pipeline where audio is first auto-captioned, which is a somewhat artificial setup. The abstract's framing ('clear advantages in two critical areas') downgrades 'comparable' T2A performance that is buried in the results

The central claim that OEA 'demonstrates superior semantic understanding of complex queries' is undercut by the paper's own Table 4: M2D-CLAP achieves the best average UIQ score (47.76 vs. 47.18), and OEA wins only on Imperative queries and hard negative metrics. Selective emphasis on favorable slices weakens the contribution's coherence

The UIQ benchmark is weaker as a 'real-world query' benchmark than claimed. Queries are generated by GPT-5.1 from captions, constrained to ±2 words of the original caption length and to reuse caption vocabulary—so they largely test reformulation style, not the 1.8-token real-world queries the paper itself cites as the motivation. Only 75 of 13,053 queries were human-validated (9 annotators), and the authors acknowledge generation was not exhaustively reviewed; a single-generator LLM introduces systematic style bias that the sample-based validation cannot fully rule out

Potential circularity in the hard negative evaluation: confusable pairs are mined using MGA-CLAP embeddings, and the paper acknowledges (Appendix N) that 'hardness' is bounded by MGA-CLAP's representational space. While dual-model filtering and human threshold calibration mitigate this, the benchmark's coverage of acoustic confusion types is unverified at scale

Efficiency gap is substantial and practically relevant: 11.5 GB peak memory and 163–666 ms/clip audio encoding vs. <1 GB and 32–107 ms for CLAP models. The paper addresses this honestly, but it limits the practical impact of the modest accuracy gains

Some presentation issues reduce clarity: the abstract and Section 5 framing oscillate between 'comparable' and 'dominant' claims; UIQ results sections (G.1–G.4) appear as empty stubs in the appendix; and the key claims require careful cross-referencing between Table 2, Table 3, Table 4, and Table 15 to verify

Novelty is moderate: adapting a multimodal LLM backbone with LoRA and InfoNCE for retrieval is a straightforward recipe; the main novel artifacts are the benchmark and metrics, whose construct validity (as noted above) has gaps

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated evaluation gap: standard audio retrieval benchmarks use caption-style queries that do not reflect real-world search behavior, and the UIQ taxonomy (conversational, reformulation, exclusionary) is a reasonable and clearly-articulated operationalization of this gap, grounded in prior work (Weck & Font 2024, Selvakumar et al. 2024).

The methodology is unusually thorough for a benchmark-plus-model paper: (1) a systematic data-leakage analysis between WavCaps training data and AudioCaps/Clotho evaluation sets (Appendix B) with concrete overlap counts and blocklist mitigation; (2) a leakage-free evaluation on MECAT; (3) human validation of the benchmark (9 annotators, 675 ratings) alongside LLM validation, with the sample-based nature of the audit honestly disclosed; (4) human calibration of hard negative mining thresholds.

The mechanism analysis (Appendix O) is a standout: rather than stopping at 'OEA is better,' the authors decompose the hard negative discrimination advantage into audio-side separation (Ablation 1, with significance tests), negation on/off effects (Ablation 2), and word-order structure sensitivity with cross-model shuffle controls (Ablations 3 and 3-X). This refines and appropriately weakens their own initial hypothesis (attributing the advantage to audio-space separation rather than LLM instruction-following), which reflects scientific good faith.

Multi-backbone validation across three LLMs from two organizations strengthens generality claims, and the observation that 3B outperforms 7B on some retrieval metrics is an interesting and practically relevant finding.

Reproducibility is well supported: benchmarks, code, and checkpoints are released; training configuration, prompts, generation parameters, and efficiency measurements are all documented in appendices; limitations are candidly discussed including compute cost, GPT-5.1 generation bias, and MGA-CLAP miner dependency.
The proposed discrimination metrics (HNSR@k, Δ-Rank, TFR) address a real deficiency of R@k for exclusionary queries, and the Figure 3 illustration makes the distinction easy to grasp.
weaknesses: The headline T2A (text-to-audio) results do not beat the state of the art: M2D-CLAP leads on AudioCaps, and the paper's framing must pivot to 'comparable performance' plus two secondary strengths (T2T and hard negative discrimination). The T2T dominance claim is about a caption-pipeline retrieval scenario whose practical importance relative to direct T2A is not fully argued; the +22% relative headline is on MECAT R@5 (47.41 vs 38.74), a narrower result than the framing suggests.

On the paper's own new benchmark (Avg UIQ, Table 4), M2D-CLAP still wins overall (47.76 vs OEA's 47.18), and OEA's advantages are concentrated in Imperative queries and Hard Neg. This means the central contribution—the UIQ benchmark—does not clearly show that the proposed model is better at real-world-style retrieval, only at a subset of query types; the honest reporting is commendable but limits the impact claim.

UIQ queries are synthetically generated by GPT-5.1 with vocabulary grounding constraints (±2 words of original captions), and only 75 of 13,053 queries were human-validated. The acknowledged divergence from real query distributions (Freesound queries average 1.8 tokens, far shorter than any UIQ type) means the benchmark itself may not capture the actual robustness gap it was designed to probe; the authors defer log-based validation to future work.

The hard negative evaluation inherits a circularity risk: negatives are mined with MGA-CLAP, and while dual-model filtering and human threshold calibration mitigate this, pairs that fall outside MGA-CLAP's acoustic similarity notion are systematically absent, as the authors themselves note. HNSR comparisons across models could partly reflect distance to the miner's embedding space.

Compute and deployment cost is substantial (3–7B backbones, 11.5 GB peak GPU memory, 163–666 ms audio encoding vs 0.7 ms for M2D-CLAP); the paper argues amortization and quantization help, but this materially weakens the case for adoption versus lightweight CLAP models given the gains are concentrated rather than dominant.

Some evidence is thin: human/LLM agreement statistics are reported per query type but annotator demographics/expertise are not described; the MECAT evaluation uses auto-generated captions whose noise level relative to human captions is acknowledged but not quantified; several appendix sections (G.1–G.4) appear as placeholders in the provided manuscript.

The novelty of the modeling contribution is modest—LoRA-adapted multimodal LLMs with symmetric InfoNCE and projection heads is a fairly standard recipe; the strongest novelty lies in the benchmark and analysis, which is where the paper's value is concentrated.
